¶
'''wat'''<sup>1</sup> (wot), ''v. t.'' An obsolete or dialectal form of ''wot.'' See ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wat'''<sup>2</sup> (wät), ''a.'' [A Scotch form of ''wet''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Wet.—'''2.''' Addicted to drinking; droughty.

'''wat'''<sup>3</sup> (wot), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''watte;'' a corruption of ''Walt,'' abbr. of ''Walter.'' Cf. ''Watt'' and ''Watts,'' as surnames.] An old familiar name for a hare.
{{smaller block|<poem>I wold my master were a ''watt''
& my boke a wyld Catt,
& a brase of grehowndis in his toppe.
I wold be glade for to se that!</poem>
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 404.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus, once concluded, out the teazers run,
And in full cry and speed, till ''Wat'''s undone.</poem>
{{right|''R. Fletcher’s Epigrams'', p. 139. (''Nares.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And when thou hast on foot the purblind hare,
Mark the poor wretch. . . .
By this, poor ''Wat,'' far off upon a hill,
Stands on his hinder legs with listening ear.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 697.}}}}

'''wat'''<sup>4</sup>'''†''', ''n.'' [Perhaps a var. of ''wight''<sup>1</sup>.] A fellow.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ffor be my thryfte I dare sweryn at this seyl,
ȝe xal fynde hym a strawnge ''watt!''</poem>
{{right|''Coventry Mysteries'', p. 294.}}}}

'''wat'''<sup>5</sup>, ''a.'' A dialectal form of ''wote'' for ''whote,'' a variant of ''hot''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wat'''<sup>6</sup> (wot), ''adv.'' [Origin obscure; prob. for ''what.''] Certainly; indeed. [Prov. Eng.]

'''watap, watapeh''' (wot′ap, wot′a-pe), ''n.'' [Amer. Ind.] The long slender roots of the white spruce, ''Picea alba,'' which are used by canoe-makers in northwestern North America for binding toge-

¶
'''watch''' (woch), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wacche'', ''wecche'', < AS. ''wæcce'', watch, watching, < ''wacan'', wake: see ''wake''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' The state of being awake; wakefulness.
{{smaller block|To lie in ''watch'' there and to think on him.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 4. 43.}}}}
'''2.''' A keeping awake for the purpose of attending, guarding, or preserving; attendance without sleep; preservative or preventive vigilance; vigil.
{{smaller block|Travellers always lie in the boat, and keep a ''watch'' to defend themselves against any attack.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 70.}}
We were told to keep good ''watch'' here all night, that there were troops of robbers on the east-side of the water who had lately plundered some boats.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, I. 84.}}}}
'''3.''' A wake. See ''wake''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 2.
{{smaller block|Oon cresset . . . to be born biforn the Baillies of the seid cite [Worcester], in the Vigille of the natiuite of Seynt John Baptiste, at the comyn ''Wacche'' of the seid cite; and the wardeyns of the seid crafte, and alle the hole crafte, shallen wayte vppon the seid Baillies in the seid Vigille, at the seid ''Wacche'', in ther best arraye harnesid.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 408.}}}}
'''4.''' Close, constant observation; vigilant attention; careful, continued notice; supervision; vigilance; outlook: as, to be on the ''watch''.
{{smaller block|<poem>When I had lost one shaft,
I shot his fellow of the self-same flight
The self-same way with more advised ''watch'',
To find the other forth. ''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 1. 142.</poem>
There [the trout] lies at the ''watch'' for any fly or minnow that comes near to him.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 75.}}}}

'''2.''' To be attentive, circumspect, or vigilant; be closely observant; notice carefully; give heed.
{{smaller block|''Watch'' and pray, that ye enter not into temptation.
{{right|Mat. xxvi. 41.}}
Rooks, ''watching'' doubtfully as you pass in the distance, rise into the air if you stop.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 62.}}}}

'''3.''' To act as a watchman, guard, sentinel, or the like; keep watch.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wat|6835|watch-clock}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''wat'''<sup>1</sup> (wot), ''v. t.'' An obsolete or dialectal form of ''wot.'' See ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wat'''<sup>2</sup> (wät), ''a.''   [A Scotch form of ''wet''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Wet.—'''2.''' Addicted to drinking; droughty.

'''wat'''<sup>3</sup> (wot), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''watte;'' a corruption of ''Walt,'' abbr. of ''Walter.'' Cf. ''Watt'' and ''Watts,'' as surnames.]   An old familiar name for a hare.
{{smaller block|<poem>I wold my master were a ''watt''
& my boke a wyld Catt,
& a brase of grehowndis in his toppe.
I wold be glade for to se that!</poem>
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 404.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus, once concluded, out the teazers run,
And in full cry and speed, till ''Wat'''s undone.</poem>
{{right|''R. Fletcher’s Epigrams'', p. 139. (''Nares.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And when thou hast on foot the purblind hare,
Mark the poor wretch. . . .
By this, poor ''Wat,'' far off upon a hill,
Stands on his hinder legs with listening ear.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 697.}}}}

'''wat'''<sup>4</sup>'''†''', ''n.''   [Perhaps a var. of ''wight''<sup>1</sup>.]   A fellow.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ffor be my thryfte I dare sweryn at this seyl,
ȝe xal fynde hym a strawnge ''watt!''</poem>
{{right|''Coventry Mysteries'', p. 294.}}}}

'''wat'''<sup>5</sup>, ''a.'' A dialectal form of ''wote'' for ''whote,'' a variant of ''hot''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wat'''<sup>6</sup> (wot), ''adv.''   [Origin obscure; prob. for ''what.'']   Certainly; indeed. [Prov. Eng.]

'''watap, watapeh''' (wot′ap, wot′a-pe), ''n.''   [Amer. Ind.]   The long slender roots of the white spruce, ''Picea alba,'' which are used by canoe-makers in northwestern North America for binding together the strips of birch-bark.

'''watch''' (woch), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wacche'', ''wecche'', < AS. ''wæcce'', watch, watching, < ''wacan'', wake: see ''wake''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' The state of being awake; wakefulness.
{{smaller block|To lie in ''watch'' there and to think on him.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 4. 43.}}}}
'''2.''' A keeping awake for the purpose of attending, guarding, or preserving; attendance without sleep; preservative or preventive vigilance; vigil.
{{smaller block|Travellers always lie in the boat, and keep a ''watch'' to defend themselves against any attack.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 70.}}}}
{{smaller block|We were told to keep good ''watch'' here all night, that there were troops of robbers on the east-side of the water who had lately plundered some boats.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, I. 84.}}}}
'''3.''' A wake. See ''wake''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 2.
{{smaller block|Oon cresset . . . to be born biforn the Baillies of the seid cite [Worcester], in the Vigille of the natiuite of Seynt John Baptiste, at the comyn ''Wacche'' of the seid cite; and the wardeyns of the seid crafte, and alle the hole crafte, shallen wayte vppon the seid Baillies in the seid Vigille, at the seid ''Wacche'', in ther best arraye harnesid.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 408.}}}}
'''4.''' Close, constant observation; vigilant attention; careful, continued notice; supervision; vigilance; outlook: as, to be on the ''watch''.
{{smaller block|<poem>When I had lost one shaft,
I shot his fellow of the self-same flight
The self-same way with more advised ''watch'',
To find the other forth. ''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 1. 142.</poem>
There [the trout] lies at the ''watch'' for any fly or minnow that comes near to him.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 75.}}}}

{{smaller block|Nor could she otherwise account for the judge’s quiescent mood than by supposing him craftily on the ''watch'', while Clifford developed these symptoms of a distracted mind.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xvi.}}}}

'''5.''' A person, or number of persons, whose duty it is to watch over the persons, property, or interests of others; a watchman, or body of watchmen; a sentinel; a sentry; guard.
{{smaller block|<poem>Such, they say, as stand in narrow lanes,
And beat our ''watch'', and rob our passengers.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., v. 3. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|Home in a coach, round by the Wall, where we met so many stops by the ''Watches'' that it cost us much time and some trouble, and more money, to every ''Watch'', to them to drink.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, III. 410.}}}}

'''6.''' The period of time during which one person or body of persons watch or stand sentinel, or the time from one relief of sentinels to another; hence, a division of the night, when the precautionary setting of a watch is most generally necessary; period of time; hour. {{smaller|The Jews, like the Greeks and Romans, divided the night into military watches instead of hours, each watch representing the period for which each separate body of sentinels remained on duty. The proper Jewish reckoning recognized only three such watches: the first (lasting from sunset till about 10 {{sc|p. m.}}), the second or ''middle watch'' (10 {{sc|p. m.}} to 2 {{sc|a. m.}}), and the third, or ''morning watch'' (from 2 {{sc|a. m.}} till sunrise). After the establishment of the Roman power they were increased to four, which were named as ''first'', ''second'', etc., or by the terms ''even'', ''midnight'', ''cock-crowing'', and ''morning'', these terminating respectively at 9 {{sc|p. m.}}, midnight, 3 {{sc|a. m.}}, and 6 {{sc|a. m.}}}}

'''7.''' ''Naut.'': (''a'') The period of time occupied by each part of a ship’s crew alternately while on duty. {{smaller|The period of time called a ''watch'' is four hours, the reckoning beginning at noon or midnight. Between 4 and 8 {{sc|p. m.}} the time is divided into two short watches, or ''dog-watches'', in order to prevent the constant recurrence of duty to the same portion of the crew during the same hours. Thus, the period from 12 to 4 {{sc|p. m.}} is called the ''afternoon watch'', from 4 to 6 the ''first dog-watch'', from 6 to 8 the ''second dog-watch'', from 8 to 12 the ''first night watch'', from midnight to 4 {{sc|a. m.}} the ''middle watch'', from 4 to 8 the ''morning watch'', and from 8 to 12 noon the ''forenoon watch''. When this alternation of watches is kept up during the 24 hours, it is termed having ''watch and watch'', in distinction from keeping all hands at work during one or more watches.}}
{{smaller block|After 2. or 3. ''watches'' more we were in 24. fadoms.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 112.}}}}
(''b'') A certain part of the officers and crew of a vessel who together attend to working her for an allotted time. {{smaller|The crew of every vessel while at sea is generally divided into two parts: the ''starboard watch'', which in the merchant service is the captain’s watch, and is often commanded by the second mate; and the ''port'' or ''larboard watch'', which in the merchant service is commanded by the chief mate. In the British and United States navies these watches are commanded by the lieutenants successively. The ''anchor-watch'' is a small watch composed of one or two men appointed to look after the ship while at anchor or in port.}}

'''8.''' Anything by which the progress of time is perceived and measured. {{smaller|(''a''†) A candle marked out into sections, each of which required a certain time to burn.}}
{{smaller block|Fill me a bowl of wine. Give me a ''watch''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 3. 63.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') A small portable timepiece or timekeeper that may be worn on the person, operated by power stored in a coiled spring, and capable of keeping time when held in any position. Watches were invented at Nüremberg about the beginning of the sixteenth century, and for a long time the wearing of a watch was considered in some degree a mark or proof of gentility. Thus Malvolio remarks in anticipation of his great fortune:}}
{{smaller block|I frown the while; and perchance wind up my ''watch'', or play with my—some rich jewel.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 5. 66.}}}}
{{smaller block|The new contrivance of applying precious stones to ''watches'' I had the good fortune to see when Mr. Facio, the inventor, and an ingenious man, and Mr. Debaufre, the workman, presented their ''watches'', to have the approbation of the Royal Society.
{{right|''W. Derham'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 173).}}}}
{{smaller block|A friend of mine had a ''watch'' given him when he was a boy, a “bull’s eye,” with a loose silver case that came off like an oyster-shell from its contents; you know them—the cases that you hang on your thumb, while the core, or the real ''watch'', lies in your hand as naked as a peeled apple.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, ii.}}}}
'''9.''' ''pl.'' A name of the trumpetleaf, ''Sarracenia flava'', probably alluding to the resemblance of the flowers to watches.—'''10.''' In ''pottery'', a trial piece of clay so placed in a kiln that it can be readily withdrawn to enable the workmen to judge by its appearance of the heat of the fire and the condition of the ware remaining in the saggars.—'''11.''' In ''hawking'', a company or flight, as of nightingales.—{{smaller|'''Beat of a watch.''' See ''beat''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Duplex watch''', a watch having two sets of teeth upon the rim of its escapement-wheel.—'''Officer of the watch.''' See ''watch-officer''.—'''Paddy’s watch.''' Same as ''paddywhack'', 3.—'''Parish watch.''' See ''parish''.—'''The Black Watch''', a semi-military organization in Edinburgh, Scotland, in the early part of the eighteenth century. From this a regiment of the British army was afterward formed, and the name was ultimately given to the 42d and 73d regiments, which are now the 1st and 2d Battalions of the Black Watch or Royal Highlanders.—'''To muster the watch.''' See ''muster''.—'''To stand a watch.''' See ''stand''.—'''Watch and ward''', the old custom of watching by night and by day in towns and cities. English writers up to the seventeenth century recognize a distinction between ''watch'' and ''ward'', the former being used to signify a watching and guarding by night, and the latter a watching, guarding, and protecting by day. Hence, when the terms were used in combination, especially in the phrase ''to keep watch and ward'', they implied a continuous and uninterrupted watching and guarding, constant vigilance and protection by night and by day.}}
{{smaller block|It ys the Strongest towne of walls, towers, Bulwerks, ''waches and wardes'' that ever I saw in all my lyff.
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|I sawe at the towne of Braxima al the artillerie brought together to y<sup>e</sup> gates of your house; I saw ''watch and warde'' kept round about your lodging.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 246.}}}}

'''watch''' (woch), ''v.''   [< ME. ''wacchen'', ''wecchen'', < AS. ''wæccan'', watch, wake: see ''wake''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', and cf. ''watch'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be awake; be or continue without sleep; keep vigil.
{{smaller block|But if necessitie compell you to ''watch'' longer then ordinary, then be sure to augment your sleepe the next morning.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 252.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As soon as I am dead,
Come all and ''watch'' one night about my hearse.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, ii. 1.}}}}

'''2.''' To be attentive, circumspect, or vigilant; be closely observant; notice carefully; give heed.
{{smaller block|''Watch'' and pray, that ye enter not into temptation.
{{right|Mat. xxvi. 41.}}}}
{{smaller block|Rooks, ''watching'' doubtfully as you pass in the distance, rise into the air if you stop.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 62.}}}}

'''3.''' To act as a watchman, guard, sentinel, or the like; keep watch.

{{smaller block|The lieutenant to-night ''watches'' on the court of guard.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 1. 219.}}}}

'''4.''' To look forward with expectation; be expectant; seek opportunity; wait.—'''5.''' To act as attendant or nurse on the sick by night; remain awake to give attendance, assistance, or the like: as, to ''watch'' with a patient in a fever.—'''6.''' To float on the surface of the water: said of a buoy.—'''To watch over,''' {{smaller|to be cautiously observant of; inspect; superintend and guard from error and danger; keep guard over.}}

{{smaller block|''Watch over'' thyself, counsel thyself, judge thyself impartially.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor.''}}}}

{{smaller block|There is abundant cause to think that every town in which the Lord Jesus Christ is worshipped hath an angel to ''watch over'' it.
{{right|''C. Mather'', Mag. Chris., Hist. Boston.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To look with close attention at or on; keep carefully and constantly in view or supervision; keep a sharp lookout on or for; observe, notice, or regard with vigilance and care; keep an eye upon.

{{smaller block|Lie not a night from home; ''watch'' me like Argus.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., v. 1. 230.}}}}

{{smaller block|They are singled out, and all opportunities ''watched'' against them.
{{right|''Bacon'', Political Fables, i., Expl.}}}}

{{smaller block|When Pitt entered Parliament, the whole political world was attentively ''watching'' the progress of an event which soon added great strength to the Opposition.
{{right|''Macaulay'', William Pitt.}}}}

'''2.''' To have in keeping; tend; guard; take care of.

<poem>Flaming ministers to ''watch'' and tend
Their earthy charge.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 156.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Lord Brampton.'' Charges? For what?
''Sable.'' First, Twenty Guineas to my Lady’s Woman for notice of your Death (a Fee I’ve before now known the Widow herself go halfs in), but no matter for that. In the next place, Ten Pounds for ''watching'' you all your long Fit of Sickness last Winter.
{{right|''Steele'', Grief A-la-Mode, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Paris ''watch’d'' the flocks in the groves of Ida.
{{right|''Broome.''}}}}
'''3.''' To look for; wait for.
{{smaller block|We will stand and ''watch'' your pleasure.
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iv. 3. 249.}}}}
'''4†.''' To take or detect by lying in wait; surprise.
{{smaller block|Nay, do not fly; I think we have ''watch’d'' you now.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5. 107.}}}}
'''5.''' In ''falconry'', to keep awake; keep from sleep, as a hawk, for the purpose of exhausting and taming it.
{{smaller block|<poem>My lord shall never rest;
I’ll ''watch'' him tame, and talk him out of patience.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 23.}}}}

'''watch-bell†''' (woch′bel), ''n.'' '''1.''' An alarm-bell.
{{smaller block|They [Russian travelers] report that the Land of Mugalla reaches from Boghar to the north sea, and hath many Castles built of Stone four-square, with Towers at the Corners cover’d with glazed Tiles; and on the Gates Alarum Bells, or ''Watch-Bells'', twenty pound weight of Metal.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Moscovia, iii.}}}}
'''2.''' The bell which is struck every half-hour on board ship to mark the time. Now called ''ship’s bell.''

'''watch-bill''' (woch′bil), ''n.'' A list of the officers and crew of a ship, as divided into watches, together with the several stations to which the men respectively belong.

'''watch-birth†''' (woch′bėrth), ''n.''   [< ''watch'', ''v.'', + obj. ''birth.'']   A midwife. [Rare.]
<poem>Th’ eternall ''Watch-births'' of thy sacred Wit.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Magnificence.}}}}

'''watch-box''' (woch′boks), ''n.'' A sentry-box.

'''watch-candle''' (woch′kan″dl), ''n.'' Same as ''watching-candle.''

{{smaller block|Were it not better for a man in a fair room to set up one great light, or branching candlestick of lights, than to go about with a small ''watch candle'' into every corner?
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, i. 45.}}}}

'''watchcase''' (woch′kās), ''n.'' '''1.''' The outer case for a watch. {{smaller|Formerly it was often a hinged cover or box fitted closely over the watch proper, and having openings through which the dial appeared and the stem or ring projected. In modern watches this feature is generally absent, and the watchcase is the metal cover, usually of gold or silver, which incloses the works.}}

{{smaller block|We now never see ''watch-cases'' made of other materials than the precious metals, or imitations thereof; but then [reign of Queen Anne] beautiful cases were made of shagreen of various colours, or tortoiseshell inlaid or studded with gold.
{{right|''J. Ashton'', Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne, I. 159.}}}}

'''2.''' Same as ''watch-pocket.''—'''3†.''' A sentry-box. [Rare.]

<poem>O thou dull god [sleep], why liest thou with the vile
In loathsome beds, and leavest the kingly couch
A ''watch-case'', or a common ’larum-bell?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iii. 1. 17.}}}}

'''watchcase-cutter''' (woch′kās-kut″ėr), ''n.'' A machine for cutting hinge-recesses in watchcases.   ''E. H. Knight.''

'''watch-clock''' (woch′klok), ''n.'' '''1†.''' An alarum.

<poem>Powrfull Need (Arts ancient Dame and Keeper,
The early ''watch-clock'' of the sloathfull sleeper).</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Handy-Crafts.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
